Linked cash can reduce loan interest and still cost more: compare the whole arrangement

Use four hypothetical charts to compare an offset-style linked balance with a cheaper loan plus separate savings, including the rate difference, forgone savings interest and a one-period fee.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare an offset interest base with a complete alternative cost

Interactive planning lab

Loan balance charged interest in the offset example$260,000
Interest avoided relative to the same offset-loan quote$197.26
Net period cost advantage of offset after the extra fee-$34.66

Original hypothetical one-period cost comparison, using identical opening debt and cash. The full-offset example keeps cash in a separate linked account, pays no interest on any linked cash, and charges loan interest on max(gross principal − linked cash, 0). Cash above the loan amount cannot produce negative loan interest. The alternative keeps the full loan interest base and earns the entered gross savings interest on the same cash. Loan quotes may differ. All rates are independently entered annual SIMPLE assumptions on actual days / fixed 365, held unchanged; no market quote, APR or actual mortgage compounding convention is reproduced. Loan principal and cash balances remain constant throughout the selected period. No installment, principal repayment, interest capitalization, savings compounding, transaction date, bank balance, tax, interest deduction or payoff horizon is calculated. The entered extra offset fee applies ONCE to the whole selected period and is not automatically prorated when days change. Cost advantage equals alternative loan interest minus separate savings interest, minus offset loan interest and extra fee; positive means lower modeled net financing cost with offset. It is not a cash receipt or portfolio return. Avoided interest at the offset quote alone is not this complete comparison. The source describes an Australian product concept; the hypothetical CAD labels establish no Canadian product availability, tax treatment or local legal rule. Actual access, linkage, full/partial offset and pricing require the product terms.

The central idea

Interest avoided at the offset loan’s own rate is not the net benefit. Compare the alternative loan’s rate, the savings interest given up and the extra fee before treating the arrangement as cheaper.

01

Separate the linked cash, the loan principal and the interest base

An offset-style arrangement links a cash account to a loan. The cash stays in the account, but the lender subtracts it from the loan balance before calculating interest. Moneysmart, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission’s consumer site, describes a mortgage offset account as a transaction account linked to a home loan, generally a variable-rate loan. Its example charges interest on an AUD 700,000 balance when an AUD 750,000 loan is paired with AUD 50,000 in the offset account.

That reduction is not a repayment. The gross loan principal is still owed, the scheduled principal payments do not disappear, and the linked cash remains a separate balance. The first chart therefore shows three different quantities: gross principal, linked cash and the balance actually charged interest. They are definitions, not additive pieces of one total.

Moneysmart also says interest on most home loans is calculated daily, with the lender subtracting the offset balance each day before calculating interest. A daily convention matters because the benefit depends on how much cash is linked on each day, not only on a month-end snapshot. This calculator simplifies that into one constant-balance period measured in actual days over a fixed 365-day year.

The source describes an Australian product. The CAD labels in this example are hypothetical and establish no Canadian availability, eligibility, tax treatment or legal rule. A reader who encounters a similar linked-balance feature should verify the actual product terms rather than assuming the mechanics carry over unchanged.

02

Treat “interest avoided” as one component, not the final saving

The default example starts with CAD 300,000 of gross principal, CAD 40,000 of linked cash, a 6% offset-loan rate, a 5.5% alternative-loan rate, 3% separate savings interest, a 30-day period and a CAD 10 extra fee. All rates are independently entered annual simple assumptions.

The offset loan charges interest on CAD 260,000 for 30 days: about CAD 1,282.19. The alternative loan charges interest on the full CAD 300,000 at 5.5%: about CAD 1,356.16. The same CAD 40,000 kept in separate savings earns about CAD 98.63 at 3%. Adding the CAD 10 fee gives an offset cost of about CAD 1,292.19, against an alternative net cost of about CAD 1,257.53.

On those assumptions the offset arrangement costs about CAD 34.66 more, even though it avoids about CAD 197.26 of interest at the offset loan’s own rate. The bridge chart reconciles the difference: CAD 197.26 avoided − CAD 123.29 rate premium on the full principal − CAD 98.63 savings interest forgone − CAD 10 fee = −CAD 34.66.

The order matters. The offset quote is half a percentage point above the alternative, and that difference applies to the whole CAD 300,000 before any offset benefit is credited. The separate savings alternative earns interest on all CAD 40,000. Only after both adjustments and the fee does the comparison show a net cost. Quoting the CAD 197.26 alone would overstate the benefit by ignoring the cheaper quote and the interest given up.

03

Compare a like-for-like loan quote and put every fee in the same period

An offset feature is not free merely because the linked cash earns no taxable interest. Moneysmart warns that some banks charge for offset features through a higher interest rate, account fees or both, and it recommends comparing those costs with the interest expected to be saved. The calculator makes the rate difference and the fee explicit rather than assuming the offset loan is priced identically to the alternative.

The extra fee is entered once for the entire selected period. Changing the day count does not automatically prorate it, because the model treats it as a flat arrangement cost already agreed for that period. A real fee may be monthly, annual, upfront or bundled into a package. Convert it to the same period as the interest comparison, and do not count the same charge twice.

If both loans carried the same rate, the rate-premium row would disappear. The comparison would still not be automatically favourable: the linked cash could have earned savings interest elsewhere, and the fee would still apply. Conversely, a lower offset quote can add value through the rate-difference row. The direction of the whole result depends on both quotes, the savings assumption, the cash amount and the fee together.

This is a one-period interest-cost comparison. It does not model installments, principal repayment, interest capitalization, savings compounding, transaction dates, taxes, interest deductibility or a full payoff horizon. Those omissions matter for a real mortgage decision, where the balance and the rate can change over many years.

04

More linked cash stops helping the loan once it covers the principal

The cash-sensitivity chart varies the amount held in the linked account or in separate savings while keeping the loan, rates, period and fee selected. The line rises while linked cash reduces a positive interest base. It peaks when linked cash equals the gross principal, because the loan interest base has reached zero. Adding more cash cannot produce negative loan interest.

Beyond that point the line falls under the model’s assumptions. The extra cash no longer reduces loan interest, while the separate-savings alternative continues to earn the entered savings rate on all of its balance. The result is a cost comparison, not a verdict that holding more than the loan balance is wrong. Cash above the loan balance may serve as an emergency reserve, a sinking fund or a daily transaction buffer.

Liquidity is a genuine difference between linked cash and an extra principal repayment. Moneysmart distinguishes an offset account, where savings remain accessible, from a redraw facility, where extra payments go onto the loan and access depends on the loan terms. The model does not treat the linked balance as a repayment, and it does not assume the cash is locked away.

Do not read the peak as a recommendation to hold exactly the loan balance. Minimum balances, spending patterns, access rules, deposit insurance, tax and the need for an emergency reserve all sit outside this arithmetic. The chart answers only how one modeled net interest cost changes with the cash amount.

05

Change both loan quotes, not just the advertised offset rate

The final matrix replaces the offset-loan quote by row and the alternative-loan quote by column, holding principal, cash, savings interest, days and fee fixed. Positive cells mean the offset arrangement has a lower modeled net cost; negative cells mean it costs more. The cells are invented combinations, not product quotes or probabilities.

The grid is useful because a headline comparison often changes one rate at a time. A lender may advertise a low offset rate while the no-offset alternative is lower still, or the reverse. Reading only the interest avoided at the offset rate hides that relationship. Reading both quotes together shows how quickly the advantage can disappear when the alternative is cheaper.

A positive cell is still conditional. It does not establish that the household will keep the same cash balance every day, that the lender will calculate interest exactly as modeled, or that the fee will remain unchanged. A negative cell does not prove the product is a bad choice in every respect; it shows that this narrow cost comparison is unfavourable under those assumptions.

The matrix also separates the question from the sales description. “Offset” describes a mechanism, not a guaranteed saving. The same mechanism can be priced well or poorly relative to the next available loan.

06

Check the linkage and the contract, not only the projected saving

An offset benefit depends on the account actually being linked and the lender actually applying it. ASIC’s 2026 review of eight Australian banks reported more than AUD 55 million in compensation for offset failures reported between September 2023 and August 2025. The accompanying REP 837 report attributed 55% of identified failures to an account opened but not linked, 22% to an account not opened and 14% to linking outside communicated timeframes, with the remaining 9% classified as other.

ASIC noted that repayments can stay the same while a customer unknowingly pays more interest, which makes the failure hard to notice. Its consumer steps are practical: confirm the account was set up, confirm it is linked to the correct loan, and confirm the interest saving appears in online banking, the app or statements. A refinance or product switch may require the account to be relinked.

Before relying on any offset-style arrangement, verify the current interest rate with and without the feature, every account and package fee, whether the offset is full or partial, how daily balances are treated, any minimum or maximum, and how access works. Confirm the tax treatment and the local availability of the product. If the feature is not available in the reader’s market, the arithmetic can still illustrate the trade-off, but it is not a product recommendation.

Finally, keep the comparison period honest. A one-month illustration cannot capture years of changing rates, principal payments and fees. Use actual statements and the contract’s own terms for a real decision, and treat this calculator as a way to organize the questions rather than as a quote, approval or advice.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Four original charts use one constant-balance CAD example and invented rates. The linked-balance mechanics come from an Australian regulator’s explanation of mortgage offset accounts. No Canadian product availability, actual quote, tax treatment, compounding convention or recommendation is shown. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope.
